title: YOU CAN BELIEVE IN GOD, LIVE A GOOD LIFE… AND STILL HEAR JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
paragraphs: YOU CAN BELIEVE IN GOD, LIVE A GOOD LIFE… AND STILL HEAR JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
The terrifying difference between being a good person and being saved—and the extraordinary grace of Jesus Christ that can change your eternity before it is too late.
What if the greatest danger to your soul isn't that you've rejected God…
But that you've convinced yourself you're already right with Him?
Read that again.

Because somewhere in this world, a man is preparing for church. He has never murdered anyone. He provides for his family. He helps people when he can. He believes in God, respects the Bible, and considers himself a decent human being.

And somewhere else, a woman is quietly proud of the life she's lived. She's honest. She's generous. She prays when things become difficult. She believes heaven exists, and if anyone deserves to go there, surely someone who has tried so hard to be good should have a place.
Neither of them thinks they're in spiritual danger.
That's what makes this so heartbreaking.
Because Jesus once described people who would stand before Him on the final day, absolutely convinced they belonged to Him.
They would not be atheists mocking His name.
They would be people calling Him Lord.
People who had done religious works.
People who believed they had every reason to be welcomed.
And yet, Jesus warned that some would hear words more devastating than anything a human heart could imagine:
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Not, “You weren't good enough compared with your neighbors.”
Not, “You failed to accomplish enough religious activities.”
But…
“I never knew you.”
Imagine spending your entire life believing you're walking toward heaven, only to discover that you had mistaken religious familiarity for a saving relationship with Jesus Christ.
That possibility should not make us rush to judge other people.
It should make us examine our own hearts.
Because the question is not merely whether you believe God exists.
The question is whether you have truly entrusted yourself to the Son of God who came to save you.
And the difference is eternal.
There is a Greek word in the New Testament that makes this warning especially uncomfortable.
In James 2:19, Scripture says:
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” — KJV
The Greek verb is πιστεύεις (pisteueis), from πιστεύω (pisteuō), meaning “to believe.”
James is confronting a kind of belief that acknowledges a theological truth without producing the obedience and transformation that accompany living faith.
Even demons recognize that God is real.
They possess accurate information about His existence.
But recognizing God's existence is not the same as being reconciled to Him.
Think about that.
You can believe there is a heaven without knowing the One who opens its doors.
You can believe Jesus lived without trusting the significance of His death and resurrection.
You can know the words of a thousand worship songs and still resist the Lord those songs proclaim.
You can defend Christianity publicly while refusing Christ privately.
And perhaps most frightening of all…
You can become so accustomed to Christian language that you stop asking whether your heart has ever truly surrendered.
But before fear overwhelms you, understand something important.
Jesus did not give these warnings because He delights in turning people away.
He gave them because He tells the truth.
And the truth, even when it wounds our pride, can become the very doorway through which grace enters.
There was once a man who approached Jesus with a question that sounded almost perfect.
He wanted to know what he needed to do to inherit eternal life.
He had respected God's commandments since his youth. By outward appearances, he was the kind of person most religious communities would celebrate.
Disciplined.
Respectable.
Morally serious.
Yet when Jesus confronted him with the cost of following Him, the man walked away grieving because he possessed great wealth.
You can read the encounter in Mark 10:17–22.
But don't overlook one extraordinary detail.
Mark 10:21 says:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.” — KJV
Jesus loved him.
Before the man walked away.
Before his attachment to wealth was exposed.
Before he demonstrated how difficult surrender would be.
Jesus loved him.
And because Jesus loved him, He refused to flatter him into a false sense of security.
Christ exposed the very thing competing for the throne of his heart.
For that man, it was wealth.
For someone else, it may be reputation.
For another, secret sin.
For another, religious pride.
For another, the desperate need to remain in control.
What is it for you?
What is the one thing you hope Jesus will never ask you to surrender?
Because sometimes the thing keeping us from wholehearted obedience isn't something society considers evil.
Sometimes it's something good that has become ultimate.
A relationship.
A career.
A dream.
A comfortable life.
Even a reputation for being a good Christian.
And when Jesus puts His finger on it, suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
Do I want Jesus Himself?
Or do I only want the blessings I hope He will give me?
There's another man in Scripture whose story may feel even closer to home.
His name was Nicodemus.
He wasn't a criminal.
He wasn't an outspoken enemy of religion.
He was a Pharisee, a teacher of Israel, and a respected religious leader.
If spiritual knowledge alone could save someone, Nicodemus would have appeared to be an excellent candidate.
He knew the Scriptures.
He understood religious customs.
He had devoted his life to studying God's law.
And yet, when he came to Jesus at night, Christ told him something that overturned his entire understanding of spiritual security.
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3, KJV
The Greek expression is γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (gennēthē anōthen).
The word anōthen can mean “again” or “from above,” and John's account draws attention to that profound reality.
Jesus was not simply telling Nicodemus to become a little more religious.
He was speaking of a birth that comes from above.
A work of God.
A new life brought about by the Spirit.
Nicodemus needed something that religious achievement could never manufacture.
He needed spiritual rebirth.
And so do we.
You cannot inherit salvation merely because your parents believed.
You cannot earn it through church attendance.
You cannot purchase it through donations.
You cannot obtain it through public recognition, charitable projects, or an impressive moral résumé.
And you cannot create it simply by deciding that you will become a better person tomorrow.
The problem goes deeper than behavior.
It reaches the human heart.
Scripture declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
All.
The respectable businessman.
The devoted mother.
The generous neighbor.
The pastor.
The missionary.
The person who has never entered a church.
And the person who has attended one every Sunday for forty years.
Every one of us stands in need of God's mercy.
That does not mean every person has committed the same sins or caused the same harm.
It means no one possesses the sinless righteousness required to stand before a holy God on the basis of personal merit.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people earning their way into heaven.
It is the story of a holy and merciful God rescuing sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say, “Become worthy enough, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save the unworthy.
He lived the sinless life we failed to live.
He willingly gave Himself on the cross for our sins.
He bore the judgment our rebellion deserved.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
Not as a symbol.
Not merely as a beautiful religious idea.
But as the risen Lord whose victory over death stands at the heart of the Christian faith.
The apostle Paul summarized the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4:
“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” — KJV
This is why salvation is not a trophy handed to the morally impressive.
It is a gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
In Greek, the word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of grace, favor, and gift.
In this passage, salvation is presented as God's gracious work, not something we earn through our accomplishments.
But don't stop reading at verse nine.
Verse ten explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because we perform good works.
We are saved by grace for a life in which good works bear witness to God's transforming power.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the price of admission.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because if your hope of heaven depends on your own goodness, how will you ever know when you have been good enough?
How many prayers would be sufficient?
How much generosity would erase your guilt?
How many acts of kindness would outweigh one lifetime of sin?
And who gets to decide?
You?
Your pastor?
Your family?
Your conscience?
No.
God has not appointed human self-confidence as the measure of righteousness.
He has revealed His righteousness in Jesus Christ.
Romans 10:9 declares:
“That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.” — KJV
This is not an invitation to repeat a formula while secretly clinging to unbelief.
It is a call to genuine faith in the crucified and risen Lord.
And genuine faith changes the direction of a life.
Not because believers become instantly flawless.
They don't.
Christians still struggle.
They still face temptation.
They still grieve over failures.
Sometimes they fall in ways that leave them ashamed to lift their faces toward heaven.
But the difference is that the Holy Spirit is at work within them, drawing them toward repentance, truth, obedience, and dependence upon Christ.
Repentance is not pretending you will never sin again.
It is turning from sin toward God, refusing to make peace with the darkness that Christ came to deliver you from.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated “repentance.” It refers to a change of mind and heart that involves a changed response to God and to sin.
It is more than momentary regret.
More than embarrassment after being caught.
More than tears caused by painful consequences.
True repentance turns toward the mercy and authority of Jesus.
And here's something the struggling believer needs to hear.
The fact that you are fighting sin does not automatically mean you are lost.
The fact that you are grieved by your failures does not mean God has abandoned you.
The fact that your spiritual growth feels painfully slow does not mean Christ has stopped working.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Your confidence must not rest in your ability to achieve perfection.
It must rest in the perfect Savior who calls you to walk in His light.
But neither should grace become an excuse to cherish the sin that nailed our Savior to the cross.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace does not simply leave us unchanged.
Perhaps you're reading this with a secret nobody knows.
A habit you've hidden.
A betrayal you've never confessed.
A bitterness you've carried for years.
An addiction that keeps pulling you backward.
A public image that looks holy while your private life is collapsing.
You know the language of faith.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know how to smile when someone asks how you're doing.
But underneath it all, there's a question you keep pushing away.
What if I know about Jesus, but I don't truly know Him?
If that question is piercing your heart, don't silence it.
Bring it into the light of Scripture.
Bring it honestly before God.
And remember that Christ's invitation is not reserved for people who have already cleaned themselves up.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Read that promise slowly.
The person who comes to Christ in genuine faith will not be turned away.
Not because their past is harmless.
Not because their sins are insignificant.
Not because God has lowered His standard of holiness.
But because Jesus is a sufficient Savior.
He receives sinners.
He forgives the repentant.
He gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And this brings us to one of the most moving scenes in all of Scripture.
Two men were being crucified beside Jesus.
Both were criminals.
Both were dying.
Neither had time to rebuild his reputation.
Neither could spend the next twenty years proving how morally improved he had become.
One continued to mock Jesus.
The other recognized his guilt and acknowledged Christ's innocence.
Then, with death approaching, he turned toward the Savior hanging beside him.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42, KJV
He had no impressive record to present.
No religious achievements to boast about.
No opportunity to undo the suffering his sins had caused.
He had nothing to offer as payment for salvation.
Only a desperate appeal to Jesus.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
What an astonishing picture of grace.
A dying sinner turns to a dying Savior.
And receives the promise of life beyond death.
The man did not earn paradise.
He was received through the mercy of Christ.
Now compare those two scenes.
The respectable rich man walked away sorrowful when Jesus confronted his deepest attachment.
The condemned criminal turned toward Jesus with nothing left to claim.
One had a morally impressive life.
The other had a criminal past.
Yet outward respectability was not what saved the first man, and past wickedness was not beyond the Savior's power to forgive the second.
The decisive issue was their response to Jesus Christ.
And that should shake every one of us.
Because there will be people in heaven whose earthly stories would have shocked respectable society.
And there may be people who were admired on earth yet never truly trusted the Savior.
We cannot identify their final destinies by appearances.
God knows the heart.
But we can hear His warning.
And we can receive His invitation.
Maybe you've been thinking, I'm a good person. I don't hurt anyone. I believe in God. Surely that's enough.
But Jesus did not say, “I am one of many possible ways.”
He said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6, KJV
Those words are exclusive in their claim.
And extraordinary in their invitation.
Because the One who declared Himself the way also gave His life to open that way for sinners.
He did not stand at a distance demanding that broken humanity climb high enough to reach Him.
He came into our brokenness.
He entered our suffering.
He endured rejection, humiliation, and crucifixion.
And He rose victorious.
This is why Jesus Christ must remain at the center of the message.
Not our platform.
Not our reputation.
Not our achievements.
Not even the number of people who applaud our ministry.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
The One who takes the guilty and offers forgiveness.
The One who calls the proud to repentance.
The One who welcomes the weary.
The One who restores the fallen.
The One who gives new life to those who could never earn it.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because every consequence of our past disappears.
Not because every wound heals overnight.
Not because following Jesus guarantees a painless life.
But because sin and shame do not have to write the final chapter of the person who belongs to Christ.
His grace is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
His resurrection is greater than the grave.
And His mercy is not exhausted by the depth of our need.
So what should you do if you're no longer certain where you stand with God?
Don't rush to manufacture an emotional experience.
Don't search for reassurance merely in how religious you look.
Don't assume that fear itself proves you're saved or lost.
Look to Jesus Christ.
Examine what you believe about Him.
Confess your sins honestly.
Turn toward Him in repentance.
Trust His death and resurrection as the basis of your salvation.
And seek to follow Him, not as a way of purchasing His love, but as the response of a heart being transformed by grace.
Second Corinthians 13:5 says:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith.” — KJV
Self-examination is not meant to trap you in endless terror.
It is meant to confront false confidence and direct you toward genuine faith.
The Christian's deepest assurance is not, “I have always been good.”
It is, “Jesus Christ is mighty to save.”
And perhaps today, for the first time, you are ready to stop trusting in your goodness and begin trusting in His.
You can speak to Him right where you are.
No stage.
No audience.
No impressive vocabulary.
Just honesty before the God who already knows your heart.

Lord Jesus, I have spent so much of my life measuring myself against other people. I have called myself good while overlooking the sins and pride within me. I confess that I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Turn my heart away from sin. Teach me to trust You, follow You, and live by Your grace. I don't want merely to know religious facts about You. I want to belong to You. Amen.
Those words are not a magical formula.
Our hope is not in the perfection of a prayer.
Our hope is in the living Christ to whom faith turns.
And if you've trusted Him, don't walk this journey alone.
Read His Word.
Pray.
Become part of a faithful, Bible-teaching church.
Seek baptism as Christ commanded.
Walk with mature believers who can encourage you, correct you, and help you grow.
And when you fall, don't run deeper into hiding.
Return to the Savior.
There is no shame in admitting that you need grace.
The tragedy is insisting that you don't.
If this message has exposed something you've been afraid to face, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You don't need to tell strangers every detail of your private struggle.
But you can let your response become a small declaration of where you want your heart to go.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from spiritual pride, secret shame, or a life of rebellion into repentance and restoration, consider sharing it.
Your story may encourage someone who believes they're too far gone to be forgiven.
Please don't let this message end with you.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who has spent years believing that being decent is the same as being saved.
Someone who goes to church but has never seriously examined the Gospel.
Someone who stopped attending church because they believed their past made them unacceptable to God.
Someone who is quietly wondering whether Jesus would still receive them.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to frighten people into religion.
But to place the truth of Christ before someone who may desperately need to hear it.
Not as a lucky charm or a measure of spiritual devotion, but as a reminder to return to the Scriptures and examine what it truly means to believe in Jesus.
Our purpose is not to gather an audience around human personalities.
It is to keep directing hearts toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, conviction, repentance, forgiveness, encouragement, and discipleship.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford to pay for it.
And that brings me to a personal invitation.

If these messages have helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you to return to prayer, strengthened your faith, or reminded you of the grace of Jesus, would you prayerfully consider helping Gospel Warrior continue and expand this work?
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
We want your decision to come from conviction and willingness, never guilt.
You are welcome to read, learn, share, and grow.
The message of Jesus Christ is not for sale.
The forgiveness He offers cannot be purchased.
The grace that saves us is not a premium membership benefit.
It is God's gift in His Son.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your encouragement to another struggling believer matters.
And if God has given you the ability and desire to help sustain this work financially, that generosity matters too.
But none of these things can take the place of knowing Jesus.
Which brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Can someone believe in God, live a good life, and still be lost?
According to the teaching of Jesus and His apostles…
Yes.
Because belief that merely acknowledges God's existence is not necessarily saving faith.
Because outward goodness cannot erase sin.
Because religious activity cannot replace spiritual rebirth.
Because salvation is found in Jesus Christ, not in our ability to impress heaven.
But here is the greater truth.
Someone who has lived a sinful, broken, shame-filled life can still be saved by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The door of mercy is not reserved for those with beautiful histories.
It is open to sinners who come to the Savior.
Remember the thief on the cross.
Remember Nicodemus, who later appeared publicly among those attending to Jesus' burial.
Remember Peter, who denied knowing Jesus and was later restored.
Remember Paul, who persecuted the church before becoming a witness to the Christ he once opposed.
Their stories were different.
Their failures were different.
Their journeys were different.
But the hope at the center of the Christian faith remained the same.
Jesus Christ.
And if you are still breathing, you should not treat God's invitation lightly.
Don't postpone repentance because you assume tomorrow is guaranteed.
Don't confuse a respectable reputation with a redeemed heart.
Don't spend your life polishing an image while neglecting the condition of your soul.
And don't believe the lie that your past is too terrible for the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
The final question is not whether the world thinks you are a good person.
It is whether your hope is in Jesus Christ.
Because when everything earthly is stripped away—your achievements, your possessions, your reputation, your applause—only one foundation will endure.
Not your goodness.
His grace.
Not your perfect record.
His finished work.
Not your ability to save yourself.
His power to save.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking words a person could ever hear are, “I never knew you.”
But the most beautiful hope a sinner can receive is that, through faith in Jesus Christ, they can truly belong to Him.
Don't spend your whole life trying to look good enough for heaven while overlooking the Savior who came to bring you home.
